newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Berisha sees bright future for troubled Albania.
newsitem.headline: Berisha sees bright future for troubled Albania.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha on Tuesday urged thousands of savers facing ruin in an investment swindle not to lose heart, predicting better times ahead, higher living standards and economic growth.

Berisha, who must seek a fresh term in office in a vote in parliament by March 9, told supporters in the ancient town of Berat that his government was taking measures to aid those worst affected by the collapse of a string of high-yield, high-risk investment schemes.

"I believe that the measures we have taken will take Albania out of the pyramid scheme spiral. There will be a boost in living standards, foreign and local investment and economic growth," he told around 1,000 cheering supporters of his right-wing Democratic Party.

Berisha arrived in the southern town by helicopter and was driven to a cinema hall amid tight security. Police took up position on roofs surrounding the cinema and plain-clothes officers mingled with the crowd outside.
While supporters inside the hall applauded Berisha's comments, he received a cool reception outside. When he waved to the crowd before getting into his car, few responded.
Some 40 percent of people in the town of 40,000 were believed to have sunk their savings into the Gjallica pyramid scheme which collapsed last month, sparking fierce protests.
Protesters set fire to the town hall, court and main police station on January 26.

"I appeal to investors who have lost (money) in the pyramid schemes not to be overpowered by desperation because what Albania has achieved under the Democratic Party...is many times bigger than the losses in the schemes," Berisha said.
His comments may cut little ice with the thousands of families across the country who have lost their life savings.
Berisha's prediction of strong economic growth to turn Albania into a developed country within the next three years belied some of the economic facts facing Europe's poorest state.
The domestic currency, the lek, has plunged some 25 percent against the dollar this year, industrial activity has come to an almost complete standstill and unemployment tops 80 percent in some areas.
Infrastructure has changed little since the fall of communism in 1990, communications are poor and roads dire.
Berisha welcomed a statement by European Union foreign ministers, saying they backed Albania's democracy.
The ministers supported moves by the European Commission to offer aid by targeting agriculture, small and medium businesses and to give technical assistance to the banking sector.
But EU ministers made clear they expected Albania to stick to democratic principles and said they would bring their views to the attention of the Albanian government.
While Berisha visited Berat, students in the southern town of Gjirokaster near the Greek border said they were boycotting classes indefinitely in protest over the financial scandal.
They said they were acting in solidarity with student hunger strikers in the southern town of Vlore, where protesters have staged peaceful daily marches for three weeks.

In the capital Tirana, plain-clothes police prevented students from holding a protest at the university campus, accusing them of being communists. One officer threatened a Reuter television cameraman with a stone and then punched him.
